title: Vessantara's children
hookLine: he gives away even his children before the reunion; Buddhists have debated this story for centuries

cards: Some stories you finish and think: wait. That can't be right. Every tradition has a few of these, and the grown-up thing isn't to skip them.
It's to sit with them. Today's part of the Vessantara story is one of those. Buddhist teachers, kings, monks and ordinary listeners have been arguing about it for about two thousand years.
So today, no tidying up. First the story, then the argument.

teach.b: In the forest, the family lives in a simple hermitage. One day, while Maddi is out gathering fruit, an old brahmin named Jujaka arrives.
His young wife wants servants, and he's come to ask Vessantara for his children, Jali and Kanhajina. The children hide in a lotus pond.

teach.h: THE FATHER GIVES THEM, AND WEEPS.
teach.b: Their father calls them out, and he gives them. Jujaka ties their hands and drives them off. The story doesn't soften it: the children cry, and Vessantara weeps.
Then the god Sakka arrives in disguise and asks for Maddi. He gives her too, and Sakka at once gives her back.

The ending is a reunion. Jujaka wanders to the capital, the grandfather king buys the children back, Jujaka dies of overeating, and the whole family returns home in joy. But the questions don't go away.
In the Questions of King Milinda, an old dialogue, the king asks the monk Nagasena straight out: wasn't this cruel to the children and the wife? Nagasena defends the gift.
The father knew the grandfather would ransom them, he says, and the gift was made for the sake of awakening.
Other Buddhists across the centuries have been less comfortable, and modern listeners, including many Buddhists, raise the same worry about the wife and children who had no say.

Some read the story as a picture of total non-attachment, never a rule for how to raise a family. Some say it shows how costly the path to becoming a Buddha is meant to be. Others simply say it hurts.
The tradition doesn't hide the argument. It keeps retelling the story, and keeps arguing.

how: Theravada Buddhists hear the whole Vessantara story at festivals and in sermons, and teachers and listeners openly discuss its hardest scenes, as the tradition's own texts already do.

games.q: you're King Milinda. you've just heard that Vessantara gave away his children. what do you ask the monk?

games.why: the king asks straight out, and Nagasena answers him. the tradition keeps the question in its own books.

practice: Let a story that troubles you come to mind, this one or one from anywhere in your life, and let the discomfort be there without solving it.

Notice the urge to decide right away, good or bad, right or wrong, and let that urge be there too. Just breathe beside the question, the way you'd sit beside a friend who is upset; you don't have to reach an answer.

wordCard.voice: Vessantara's children. Jali and Kanhajina, given away and brought home again, at the heart of Buddhism's longest argument about a story.

orig.note: Pali: a perfection; Vessantara's life is said to complete the perfection of giving.

carryVoice: Your line: the tradition argues too. Even King Milinda asked the hard question out loud. Until tomorrow.
